findings.title: Validator has a side effect: should_block? writes to the DB on every validation
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` increments `match_count` and saves the record. It is called from inside a validator, which runs on every `valid?`, not only on save. In `UsersController#create`, `user.valid?` runs and then `user.save` runs it again, so a single signup attempt bumps `match_count` twice. Any other `valid?` call also inflates the count. Validations should not write to the database. Counting also happens even when the user is never created, and inside a validation context it can be rolled back or can leave the statistics inconsistent. The counting should happen only on an actual rejected save, or be explicit and separate from validation.

findings.title: Non-atomic read-modify-write of match_count
findings.body: `record.match_count += 1` followed by `save` is a read-modify-write in Ruby. Concurrent signups with the same blocked email load the same count and overwrite each other, so increments are lost. Use an atomic `update_all`/`increment_counter` instead. The `save` return value is also ignored.

findings.title: Email lookup is case-sensitive and not normalized
findings.body: `where(email: email)` is an exact match, and neither the stored value nor the lookup is downcased or stripped. `Bad@Spam.com` therefore bypasses a block on `bad@spam.com`. The rest of the codebase normalizes with `Email.downcase`. Blocklist bypass is trivial.

findings.title: Nil value is not guarded and the blocked check runs on every email change
findings.body: `validates :email, email: true` has no `allow_nil`, so `value` can be nil (presence already fails in that case). `email_in_restriction_setting?` then does `nil =~ regexp`, which works, but `BlockedEmail.should_block?(nil)` runs a pointless query. More importantly, the validator is also triggered by `email_changed?` in flows like `change_email` and `create_for_email`, where the side-effecting counter is bumped in unintended contexts.

findings.title: values hash is built from user.attributes and exposes raw state
findings.body: The failure response now returns `user.attributes.slice(...)` and the full `errors` hash. The client uses `result.errors.email` to add any email-related error (including a plain uniqueness error) to `rejectedEmails`. It is then reported as the generic 'invalid' message, which hides the real server error reason. The client does not distinguish the blocked error from other errors.

findings.title: rejectedEmails array is shared across all controller instances
findings.body: `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is declared on the prototype in `extend`, so one array instance is shared by all instances and persists across modal opens. Rejected emails are never cleared. Initialize it in `init` instead.

findings.title: Rejected-email message is the generic 'invalid' text
findings.body: A server-rejected email (blocked or domain-not-allowed) is shown as `user.email.invalid`, which misleads the user. A server-provided message should be used. Also, `rejectedEmails.@each` is not a valid dependent key form; use `rejectedEmails.[]`.

findings.title: Validator spec is incomplete
findings.body: The spec stubs `should_block?` and does not cover the whitelist/blacklist branches that were moved here from `User`. The old `user_spec` coverage may now be only indirect. It also does not test that blocking is skipped when a domain error already exists. There is no integration test showing a user with a blocked email fails validation, or that `valid?` repeated does not double count.
